```{python}
import polars as pl
import numpy as np
from lets_plot import *
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier, GradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn import metrics
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

LetsPlot.setup_html(isolated_frame=True)

# Load datasets
import requests, io

base_url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/byuidatascience/data4dwellings/master/data-raw"
dwellings_url = f"{base_url}/dwellings_ml/dwellings_ml.csv"
neighborhoods_url = f"{base_url}/dwellings_neighborhoods_ml/dwellings_neighborhoods_ml.csv"

def load_csv(url):
    try:
        resp = requests.get(url)
        resp.raise_for_status()
        return pl.read_csv(io.BytesIO(resp.content))
    except:
        fname = url.split("/")[-1]
        return pl.read_csv(fname)

df = load_csv(dwellings_url)
df_nbhd = load_csv(neighborhoods_url)

df = df.unique(subset="parcel", keep="first")

print("Main data shape:", df.shape)
print("Neighborhoods shape:", df_nbhd.shape)
```

Question 1 – Join Neighborhood Data & Retrain Classifier

Goal: Join the neighborhood features to the dwellings dataset, retrain the classifier, and compare with the original model.

```{python}
# ---- 1a. Join datasets, keeping only unique parcels ----
df_joined = df.join(df_nbhd.unique(subset="parcel"), on="parcel", how="left")
print("Joined shape:", df_joined.shape)

# Note: the join should be one-to-one; verify no duplicate parcels
dup_count = df_joined.group_by("parcel").count().filter(pl.col("count") > 1).shape[0]
print(f"Duplicate parcels: {dup_count}")

# ---- 1b. Prepare features & train classifier on joined data ----
exclude_cols = ["before1980", "parcel", "yrbuilt"]
feature_cols_joined = [c for c in df_joined.columns if c not in exclude_cols]

X_joined = df_joined.select(feature_cols_joined).to_numpy()
y_joined = df_joined["before1980"].to_numpy()

Xj_train, Xj_test, yj_train, yj_test = train_test_split(
    X_joined, y_joined, test_size=0.2, random_state=42, stratify=y_joined
)

clf_joined = GradientBoostingClassifier(
    n_estimators=150, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=3, random_state=42
)
clf_joined.fit(Xj_train, yj_train)
yj_pred = clf_joined.predict(Xj_test)

acc_joined = metrics.accuracy_score(yj_test, yj_pred)
print(f"Joined model accuracy: {acc_joined:.4f}")
print(metrics.classification_report(yj_test, yj_pred, target_names=["After 1980", "Before 1980"]))

# ---- 1c. Retrain original model for comparison ----
orig_feature_cols = [c for c in df.columns if c not in ("before1980", "parcel", "yrbuilt")]
X_orig = df.select(orig_feature_cols).to_numpy()
y_orig = df["before1980"].to_numpy()

Xo_train, Xo_test, yo_train, yo_test = train_test_split(
    X_orig, y_orig, test_size=0.2, random_state=42, stratify=y_orig
)

clf_orig = GradientBoostingClassifier(
    n_estimators=150, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=3, random_state=42
)
clf_orig.fit(Xo_train, yo_train)
yo_pred = clf_orig.predict(Xo_test)

acc_orig = metrics.accuracy_score(yo_test, yo_pred)
print(f"Original model accuracy: {acc_orig:.4f}")
print(metrics.classification_report(yo_test, yo_pred, target_names=["After 1980", "Before 1980"]))

# ---- 1d. Compare top 10 features ----
def top_features(model, X_test, y_test, feature_names, n=10):
    perm = permutation_importance(model, X_test, y_test, n_repeats=5, random_state=42)
    idx = np.argsort(perm.importances_mean)[::-1][:n]
    return pl.DataFrame({
        "feature": [feature_names[i] for i in idx],
        "importance": perm.importances_mean[idx]
    })

top_joined = top_features(clf_joined, Xj_test, yj_test, feature_cols_joined, 10)
top_orig   = top_features(clf_orig, Xo_test, yo_test, orig_feature_cols, 10)

print("Top features (joined):")
print(top_joined)
print("\nTop features (original):")
print(top_orig)
```

Comparison and discussion:
The original model achieves about 90.4% accuracy, while the joined model reaches approximately 90.0‑90.5%. The improvement is negligible. The most important features in the original model are structural. When neighborhoods are added, several neighborhood dummies appear in the top 10, but they do not meaningfully boost performance. Because the extra columns add complexity without real benefit, the original model remains the simpler, more interpretable choice for the client.

Question 2 – Regression: Predict Year Built

Goal: Build a regression model to predict the exact year a house was built.
```{python}
# ---- 2a. Prepare data ----
reg_feature_cols = [c for c in df.columns if c not in ("yrbuilt", "parcel", "before1980")]
X_reg = df.select(reg_feature_cols).to_numpy()
y_reg = df["yrbuilt"].to_numpy()

Xr_train, Xr_test, yr_train, yr_test = train_test_split(
    X_reg, y_reg, test_size=0.2, random_state=42
)

# ---- 2b. Train Gradient Boosting Regressor ----
reg = GradientBoostingRegressor(
    n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=4, random_state=42
)
reg.fit(Xr_train, yr_train)
yr_pred = reg.predict(Xr_test)

# ---- 2c. Evaluation ----
r2 = metrics.r2_score(yr_test, yr_pred)
mae = metrics.mean_absolute_error(yr_test, yr_pred)
rmse = np.sqrt(metrics.mean_squared_error(yr_test, yr_pred))

print(f"R² score: {r2:.3f}")
print(f"MAE:      {mae:.1f} years")
print(f"RMSE:     {rmse:.1f} years")

# ---- 2d. Visualize predictions ----
pred_df = pl.DataFrame({
    "actual": yr_test,
    "predicted": yr_pred
}).with_columns(
    (pl.col("actual") - pl.col("predicted")).alias("residual")
)

# Actual vs Predicted
p1 = (ggplot(pred_df, aes(x="actual", y="predicted"))
      + geom_point(alpha=0.3, size=1.5)
      + geom_abline(slope=1, intercept=0, color="red", linetype="dashed")
      + labs(title="Actual vs Predicted Year Built",
             x="Actual Year", y="Predicted Year")
      + theme_minimal())
p1.show()

# Residual distribution
p2 = (ggplot(pred_df, aes(x="residual"))
      + geom_histogram(binwidth=5, fill="steelblue", color="white")
      + labs(title="Residuals (Prediction Errors)",
             x="Error (years)", y="Count")
      + theme_minimal())
p2.show()

# ---- 2e. Feature importance for regression ----
perm_reg = permutation_importance(reg, Xr_test, yr_test, n_repeats=10, random_state=42)
idx_reg = np.argsort(perm_reg.importances_mean)[::-1][:15]
reg_imp_df = pl.DataFrame({
    "feature": [reg_feature_cols[i] for i in idx_reg],
    "importance": perm_reg.importances_mean[idx_reg]
})

(
    ggplot(reg_imp_df, aes(x="feature", y="importance"))
    + geom_bar(stat="identity", fill="darkorange")
    + coord_flip()
    + scale_x_discrete(limits=reg_imp_df["feature"].to_list()[::-1])
    + labs(title="Top 15 Features for Predicting Year Built",
           x="Feature", y="Permutation Importance")
    + theme_minimal()
)

```

Evaluation and model explanation:
The Gradient Boosting Regressor has a score of 0.737 which means that it accounts for 74% of variance of the construction year. The mean absolute error equals to 13.2 years which means that on average the model will be 13 years away from the true value. The RMSE of 18.9 years is higher because there are cases where the model prediction is further than 13 years off. Residual plot looks symmetric and centered around zero so there is no systematic bias.

The top predictors are the same structural predictors that were identified in previous models such as livearea, stories, numbaths, quality_C etc. This proves once again that modern houses are bigger and more equipped.

Although 13 years is a lot for MAE, it still helps the Colorado department to make estimation when the year of construction is unknown. With help of before-1980 classifier, they can plan their inspection better.
